evidence_notes.finding: A three-role human-in-the-loop agent pipeline (AI Planner, AI Coding, Human) deployed inside Atlassian JIRA performed far worse on proprietary enterprise issues than on SWE-bench Verified (30% vs 86% file-localization recall; 30% vs 45% code similarity), showing that open-source benchmark results do not transfer to enterprise contexts. Human feedback at each stage recovered usefulness: 82% of generated plans were approved, 25% of code generations became pull requests, and 59% of those merged.
evidence_notes.quote: These results highlight the success of the HULA framework where human feedback is incorporated into practice.

extraction.framework: HULA (Human-in-the-loop LLM-based Agents), GPT-4 backbone, deployed in Atlassian JIRA
extraction.agent_count: 3 (AI Planner Agent, AI Coding Agent, Human Agent)
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Verified (500 issues) plus an internal Atlassian dataset of 369 JIRA issues; online evaluation on 663 real-world JIRA issues
extraction.baseline: offline generation without human feedback vs online generation with human feedback; leaderboard comparison against SWE-agent Claude
extraction.key_results: Workflow completion for 97% (SWE-bench) and 100% (internal) of issues; SWE-bench: 86% average file-localization recall, 84% perfect file localization, 45% code similarity, 31% perfect unit-test pass; internal dataset: 30% recall, 15% perfect localization, 30% high code similarity. Online: plans generated for 527/663 issues, 82% plan approval, 25% raised-PR rate, 59% merged-PR rate (56 merged PRs). Survey: 41% agreed plans matched the issue description, 61% agreed generated code was easy to read and modify.
extraction.limitations: Construct validity of LLM-as-a-Judge code similarity (mitigated by 0.7 correlation with 203 human-scored issues); external validity limited to Atlassian JIRA and may not generalize; internal validity tied to a single GPT-4 backbone; implementation details withheld for industrial confidentiality; authors argue unit-test pass rates alone are an inadequate measure of functional correctness.

evidence_notes.finding: A hierarchical supervisor/specialist collaboration framework reached 90% goal success rate across three enterprise domains, while an equivalently tool-equipped single agent regressed by up to 37 absolute points (0.53 vs 0.90 in the software-development domain), with single-agent trajectories showing more tool-parameter hallucination and incorrect tool choice; the gain was bought with substantially higher latency (168.7s vs 52.6s per session in the software domain).
evidence_notes.quote: In the single-agent setting, we observe an absolute regression of up to 37%.

extraction.framework: MAC (multi-agent collaboration framework, AWS Bedrock) with inter-agent communication, payload referencing, and dynamic routing
extraction.agent_count: 1 supervisor agent plus multiple specialist agents, with hierarchy depth greater than one
extraction.benchmark: 90 handcrafted assertion-based scenarios across Travel, Mortgage, and Software development domains (publicly released)
extraction.baseline: single agent given the union of all specialist tools; a widely adopted open-source task-automation framework (OSF)
extraction.key_results: Overall goal success rate 0.90 in all three domains with Claude 3.5 Sonnet supervisor and specialists, vs single agent 0.60 (Travel), 0.80 (Mortgage), 0.53 (Software) — up to 37 points absolute regression. Payload referencing raised Software GSR from 0.73 to 0.90 (23% relative) while cutting communication overhead per turn 27% (48.78s to 35.44s) and output tokens per communication 30% (539 to 374). Routing mode: 0.90-0.92 classification accuracy, 0.00-0.03 false switch rate, 627-751ms turn-level overhead. MAC beat the open-source framework substantially (e.g. Software 0.77 vs 0.40).
extraction.limitations: Multi-agent coordination adds large latency in complex domains (Software user-perceived turn latency up to 168.73s vs 52.61s single-agent), needing further optimization for time-sensitive applications; evaluation relies on LLM judges plus simulated users and simulated tool execution rather than real users; only centralized hierarchical mechanisms are studied, with decentralized coordination left as future work.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 120 trajectories and 2,822 LLM interactions from three single-agent SE systems, failed runs are distinguished by repetitive non-adaptive action cycles, result-insensitive next actions, and rare but costly thought-action misalignments; even a single misalignment correlated with failure or greatly increased cost (one bug extended from iteration 6 to iteration 38).
evidence_notes.quote: Repetition wastes iterations and may induce unproductive loops, as also observed in RQ2.

extraction.framework: RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover (V1), and OpenHands, unified into a common thought-action-result trajectory format
extraction.agent_count: single-agent systems; 3 distinct agents studied, 40 trajectories each
extraction.benchmark: Defects4J (RepairAgent) and SWE-bench Lite (AutoCodeRover, OpenHands); 120 trajectories, 2,822 LLM interactions
extraction.baseline: successful vs failed trajectories within and across the three agents
extraction.key_results: Thought-action misalignment is rare (1.3-3.7%) but strongly associated with failure and higher cost; consecutive action repetition is several times higher in failing trajectories (e.g. RepairAgent 6.1% success vs 13.6% failure; AutoCodeRover 0.0% vs 8.8%); no-influence result-action links rise in failures (1.2% vs 6.2% RepairAgent; 4.9% vs 14.6% AutoCodeRover); test-driven repair agents produce longer, token-intensive failing trajectories while AutoCodeRover's retrieve-locate-fix workflow is more efficient; successful sequences balance exploration, explanation, fix generation, and testing.
extraction.limitations: Potential subjectivity in manual annotation and classification despite partial inter-annotator agreement; only three bug-fixing agents, which do not cover all SE tasks or real deployments; the agents use different backbone models, complicating fair comparison; sampled trajectories may miss rare behaviours; analyses show correlation, not causality.

evidence_notes.finding: Repeating one identical prompt ten times through ChatDev's seven-role waterfall chat chain produced working code only 70% of the time, with 30% failing on compilation errors and three hallucination cases surviving multi-agent review, showing that cross-agent verification does not guarantee code quality.
evidence_notes.quote: However, despite these filters, there were three cases of hallucinations where the code, although validated, was inconclusive.

extraction.framework: ChatDev (waterfall chat-chain multi-agent framework) with GPT-4
extraction.agent_count: seven expert agents (roles including programmer, reviewer, tester across design, coding, testing, documentation phases)
extraction.baseline: traditional manual development and a prior ChatDev-based study used as a qualitative reference point
extraction.key_results: 10 identical runs of a Snake-game generation prompt gave a 70% effectiveness rate; 3 of 10 outputs failed with compilation errors. Successful runs completed in about five iterations, produced 43-116 lines of code plus seven documents, consumed 14,614-31,352 tokens, cost roughly $0.025-$0.051 per game, and took 110-249 seconds (average 156.8s). Successful games scored 7-10/10 on a seven-aspect subjective evaluation matrix; failed runs scored 0/10 on all aspects.
extraction.limitations: A single trivial task with a subjective, author-applied quality rubric; hallucinations persisted despite multiple reviewing agents and were the primary system limitation on more complex tasks; agent-level knowledge is generic and needs fine-tuning per domain; MAS-level adaptation requires specialized expertise; the study did not modify or propose a new MAS.

evidence_notes.finding: Three popular planner/code-generator/executor agent frameworks completed only about half of 34 programmable tasks, and a 19-cause three-tier failure taxonomy (planning, execution, response generation) derived from 104 failures across 204 runs showed the most common problems were improper task decomposition, failed self-refinement loops, and context/format issues rather than raw model weakness; the weaker GPT-4o mini backbone often beat GPT-4o because of GPT-4o 'overthinking'.
evidence_notes.quote: Surprisingly, the smaller GPT-4o-mini outperforms, especially in web crawling tasks, indicating that simpler models can remain highly competitive.

extraction.agent_count: 3 core roles per framework (planner, code generator, executor)
extraction.benchmark: custom 34-task benchmark covering web crawling, data analysis (from DABench), and file operations, with human-verified ground truth and exact-match success
extraction.baseline: cross-framework comparison and cross-backbone comparison (GPT-4o vs GPT-4o mini)
extraction.key_results: Approximately 50% overall task completion. GPT-4o: TaskWeaver 50.00%, MetaGPT 47.06%, AutoGen 38.24%; GPT-4o mini: TaskWeaver 58.82%, MetaGPT 50.00%, AutoGen 50.00%. Web crawling was hardest (as low as 16.67%). Success rate is zero for the first two iterations, improves rapidly between iterations 3 and 10, and yields only marginal gains beyond 10. 19-cause, three-tier failure taxonomy built from 104 failures over 204 runs; frequent causes include improper task decomposition, failed self-refinement causing infinite loops, tool-use knowledge gaps, incorrect API usage, context window loss, formatting issues, and max-round exhaustion.
extraction.limitations: Only 34 tasks, three frameworks, and two backbone models; success requires exact match to the ground-truth answer, excluding tasks that resist automated evaluation (e.g. front-end generation); tasks were pre-filtered to be at least partially solvable; failure labels come from manual annotation by three authors.

evidence_notes.finding: Two role-playing agents driven by inception prompting beat a gpt-3.5-turbo single-shot solution in 76.3% of human comparisons and 73-76% of GPT-4 comparisons, but autonomous cooperation exhibited four recurring coordination failures: role flipping, instruction repetition, flake replies, and infinite message loops.
evidence_notes.quote: Examples we encountered in our preliminary analysis include role flipping, assistant repeating instructions, flake replies, and infinite loop of messages.

extraction.framework: CAMEL role-playing framework with inception prompting and a task specifier
extraction.agent_count: 2 (AI Assistant and AI User) plus a task-specifier agent
extraction.benchmark: 100 AI Society tasks and 100 Code tasks judged by humans and GPT-4; HumanEval and HumanEval+ for the fine-tuned CAMEL-7B model
extraction.baseline: gpt-3.5-turbo single-shot solution; LLaMA-7B and Vicuna-7B for the code benchmarks
extraction.key_results: Human evaluation on AI Society: CAMEL wins 76.3%, gpt-3.5-turbo 10.4%, draw 13.3%. GPT-4 evaluation: AI Society 73.0% vs 23.0%; Code 76.0% vs 24.0%. CAMEL-7B reached HumanEval pass@1 14.0 (pass@100 57.9) vs LLaMA-7B 10.5 (36.5) and Vicuna-7B 11.0 (42.9), and HumanEval+ 12.2 vs 9.9. Termination rules were needed for role reversal, no-instruct rounds, token limits, and a 40-message cap because cost grows quadratically with conversation length. Four documented cooperation failure modes: role flipping, assistant repeating instructions, flake replies, infinite loops.
extraction.limitations: Evaluating the large and diverse generated task set would require many domain experts, so coverage is partial; OpenAI API cost limits the scale of the study; human and LLM evaluators may be biased or unreliable (e.g. preference for longer answers); only two-agent settings were studied; generated data and the fine-tuned model may contain false information; unaligned agents pose misuse risks.

evidence_notes.finding: Splitting repair into a Code Teacher that reads compiler bug reports and a Code Learner that applies the resulting Chain-of-Repair beat GPT-3.5 by roughly 18% on code generation and 4.3% on translation, and outperformed both self-repair (Self-Debug, Self-Refine) and multi-agent Self-Collaboration, showing external compiler grounding matters more than agent count.
evidence_notes.quote: The experimental results show that code repair is more effective than directly prompting LLMs to generate codes.

extraction.framework: INTERVENOR (INTERactiVE chaiN Of Repair) with Code Learner and Code Teacher agents plus compiler feedback
extraction.agent_count: 2 LLM agents (Code Learner, Code Teacher) plus a compiler/judge in the loop
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval-X (C++/Java/JS), DS-1000, and the new CodeError repair benchmark (4,463 Python instances)
extraction.baseline: GPT-3.5 zero-shot, Few-Shot, CoT, Self-Refine, Error Msgs, Self-Debug, Self-Collaboration, and open code LLMs
extraction.key_results: HumanEval pass@1 75.6 vs GPT-3.5 60.3, Self-Debug 73.8, Self-Collaboration 74.4; MBPP 69.8 vs 39.8; HumanEval-X C++/Java/JS 67.1/68.3/67.1 vs 52.4/50.6/54.3; DS-1000 39.7 vs 29.7; code translation 89.8/75.6/85.4/88.3 vs 84.3/71.5/81.7/84.6. On CodeError, single-turn CoR reaches 15.9 and multi-turn 21.7 vs Self-Refine 5.2 and Error Msgs 9.8. Best results after only three repair turns. Pairing a weaker Code Learner with a stronger Code Teacher improves results (CodeLlama-7B learner: 32.9 with self-teaching vs 36.6 with GPT-3.5 teacher).
extraction.limitations: Effectiveness depends heavily on the foundation model's proficiency in code error analysis and repair, and degrades with less capable LLMs; for purely logical errors the compiler must rely on test cases, so results are tied to the quality and coverage of those test cases.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 19 LLMs, runtime execution debugging alone captured almost all of the accuracy benefit (63.86% vs 64.82% for the full Analyst-Coder-Tester plus debugger chain, a statistically insignificant 0.96% gap), while adding agents multiplied latency (7.68 to 68.42 minutes) and degraded robustness under expanded test coverage, leading the authors to recommend simple agentic systems with debugging over complex multi-agent architectures.
evidence_notes.quote: AC and ACT showed substantial robustness drops (129.27 and 118.51), showing that agentic interaction introduces fragility.

extraction.framework: ACT (Analyst-Coder-Tester multi-agent collaboration) chained with a runtime execution Debugger
extraction.agent_count: 2-3 LLM agents (Analyst, Coder, Tester) with up to 3 collaboration iterations
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval and HumanEval+ (pass@1), evaluated over 19 LLMs
extraction.baseline: Basic one-shot prompting, AC (Analyst-Coder), ACT, Debugger only, and AC + Debugger
extraction.key_results: HumanEval mean accuracy: ACT+Debug 64.82%, Debug alone 63.86%, ACT alone 57.16%, Basic 56.48%. ACT+Debug significantly beats ACT but not Debug alone (+0.96%, not significant at alpha=0.15). Gains from chaining are largest when the two techniques perform comparably. Robustness drop from HumanEval to HumanEval+: Basic 90.83, Debugger only 107.84, AC+Debugger 110.41, ACT 118.51, AC 129.27, ACT+Debugger 137.74. Latency: Basic 7.68 min (54.09%), AC 20.89 min (53.34%), ACT 48.47 min (54.04%), Debugger 31.11 min (61.02%), AC+Debugger 38.42 min (61.7%), ACT+Debug 68.42 min (61.195%).
extraction.limitations: Evaluation restricted to HumanEval/HumanEval+ Python function-level tasks and to functional accuracy plus a rigor proxy; a permissive significance level (alpha=0.15) was used to detect small gains; broader programming domains, additional code-quality metrics beyond functional accuracy, and adaptive combination strategies are left to future work.

evidence_notes.finding: A critical review of 20+ primary studies frames an 'Agentless Paradox': structured non-agentic pipelines match or beat autonomous single- and multi-agent systems on SWE-bench at up to an order of magnitude lower cost (Agentless 1.0 27.3% at $0.34/issue vs SWE-search MCTS 23.0% at ~$4.00), and base-model choice explains more variance than architecture; the review also warns that multi-agent debate reinforces rather than corrects correlated errors when all agents share one base model.
evidence_notes.quote: When many agents make the same mistake, we call it a correlated error.

extraction.benchmark: reviewed benchmarks: HumanEval, MBPP, AgentBench, SWE-bench / Lite / Verified, Multi-SWE-bench, TheAgentCompany, SWE-bench Pro
extraction.baseline: Agentless structured pipelines and RAG baselines compared against single-agent ReAct, multi-agent collaborative, AST-augmented, MCTS-enhanced, and open-platform agents
extraction.key_results: Six architectural classes compared. Resolution rates rose from under 5% at SWE-bench's 2023 launch to over 75% on SWE-bench Verified by 2025. Agentless 1.0 (27.3% Lite, $0.34/issue) beat SWE-search (23.0%, ~$4.00) by 4.3 points at ~12x lower cost; swapping GPT-4o for Claude 3.5 Sonnet inside Agentless lifted Lite resolution from 27.3% to 40.7% (49% relative), attributing gains to the model rather than the architecture. Cost per resolved issue spans $0.34 to $10+ for similar accuracy. Six failure modes with prevalence and mitigation effectiveness: hallucination (very high), context overflow (high), test overfitting (high), over-engineering (medium), inter-agent errors (medium), security boundary violations (low-medium).
extraction.limitations: A narrative critical review of more than 20 primary studies rather than a systematic meta-analysis, with rounded or estimated per-issue costs; the review itself flags unresolved ecological validity, temporal data leakage from pre-training corpora, benchmark saturation at the high end, adversarial robustness, and safety auditing as open gaps; resolution rate as a metric hides test overfitting and regression-inducing patches.

evidence_notes.finding: A mixed-method comparison of open-source MAS frameworks found good coverage of foundational MAS concepts (roles, coordination rules, message handling) but immature telemetry, benchmarking, and human-in-the-loop support; on a README summarization task no framework dominated statistically (Dify ROUGE-L 0.479 vs Semantic Kernel 0.472, p>0.05) while completion time varied significantly.
evidence_notes.quote: However, despite these differences, no single framework consistently outperforms the others; the effectiveness largely depends on the specific context in which the framework will be employed.

extraction.framework: AutoGen, AutoGPT, Dify, Semantic Kernel, Semantic Kernel Chat (selected from 20 screened MAS frameworks), each re-implementing the Metagente teacher-student use case
extraction.agent_count: 4 LLM-based agents in the replicated Metagente teacher-student loop; 3-9 not applicable
extraction.benchmark: GitHub README.MD summarization with prompt-optimization datasets TS_10 and TS_50, scored with ROUGE-1/2/L and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests
extraction.key_results: Mean ROUGE on TS_10: Dify 0.515/0.352/0.479, Semantic Kernel 0.505/0.344/0.472, AutoGen 0.488/0.294/0.441, AutoGPT 0.473/0.275/0.428, Semantic Kernel Chat 0.472/0.278/0.427; Dify and Semantic Kernel are statistically indistinguishable (p>0.05). Frameworks cover coordination rules, role/behaviour specification, and message handling, but lack benchmarking, monitoring/telemetry, and human-in-the-loop integration. Lessons learned: monitoring capabilities are in their infancy, agent communication protocols (MCP, A2A) are crucial, empirical MAS metrics are missing, and VectorDB is the common long-term memory solution. Challenges: tool incompleteness (notably AutoGPT documentation and bugs) and limited low-code frameworks.
extraction.limitations: Qualitative assessment rests on the authors' subjective experience and may be biased; only a limited number of frameworks were analysed, restricting generalization; task-specific analysis covered a single optimization/summarization task; only one model provider (OpenAI) was used; ROUGE metrics may not adequately capture MAS performance; industrially adopted but unpublished frameworks were excluded.

evidence_notes.finding: Adding a deterministic Evidence Anchoring step (normalized Levenshtein fuzzy matching) plus a ConsistencyManager agent to a multi-agent LLM reviewer let CAPRA satisfy 88.8% of eight rubric criteria under strict two-rater aggregation, but reliability collapsed on the interpretive 'Grounded Issues' criterion (50% strict pass, kappa 0.348), so human oversight remains necessary for subjective dimensions.
evidence_notes.quote: Importantly, the Evidence Anchoring mechanism acted as a verification gate: findings that could not be verified against the source text were filtered out, substantially reducing ungrounded critiques.

extraction.framework: CAPRA (Configurable Architecture Proficiency Report Assessment) with gpt-4o vision extraction and gpt-5.1 analysis agents
extraction.agent_count: multiple specialized agents (multi-modal extraction, dimension-specific analyzers, ConsistencyManager); exact count not stated
extraction.benchmark: custom eight-criterion binary rubric (A1-D1) applied by two human raters to 10 student software-architecture reports, plus 10 separate reports for knowledge-base construction
extraction.baseline: manual instructor review estimated at 30-45 minutes per report
extraction.key_results: 88.8% criteria pass under strict (min of two raters) aggregation and 91.9% lenient; raw inter-rater agreement 93.75% over 80 decisions with Cohen's kappa 0.582 (moderate). Perfect 100% pass on use-case completeness, test types/coverage, feature validation, and actionable recommendations; weakest on Grounded Issues (65% lenient, 50% strict, kappa 0.348) and Architecture & Design Patterns (85%/80%, kappa 0.615). Mean processing 248s (SD 73.1s) at about $0.44 per report, a 7.2-10.8x speedup over manual review. The knowledge base was auto-generated from 680 raw mentions via HDBSCAN clustering with no manual rubric authoring.
extraction.limitations: Both raters were paper authors, risking evaluator bias; only top-scoring reports were used, inflating pass rates and never stressing the system with deficient deliverables; 10 reports from one course at one university; a single proprietary model (gpt-5.1) creates cost and reproducibility dependencies and residual non-determinism; binary Pass/Fail rubric loses granularity; Evidence Anchoring thresholds were set empirically without sensitivity analysis; observed cross-lingual drift where Italian source documents caused mixed-language output.

evidence_notes.finding: A decentralized DAG-structured framework with retrieval-augmented agent evolution outperformed centralized multi-agent baselines such as MetaGPT and GPTSwarm and matched or beat strong single-agent prompting, but the heterogeneity ablation showed role/model diversity actually hurts small teams and only pays off at larger scale, and several multi-agent baselines fell far below single-agent prompting.
evidence_notes.quote: With 3 agents, the fully homogeneous setting performs best, while introducing either model or skill diversity reduces accuracy, suggesting uniform reasoning is more effective in small teams.

extraction.framework: AgentNet, a decentralized RAG-based DAG framework with dynamic routing and adaptive expertise evolution
extraction.agent_count: 3 agents in the main comparison; scaling experiments with 3, 5, 7, and 9 agents
extraction.benchmark: MATH (140 test problems), BBH (100 test problems), API-Bank function calling (100 test tasks)
extraction.baseline: single-agent: Direct, ReAct, Synapse, Self-Consistency, Self-Refinement; multi-agent: MorphAgent, MetaGPT, AFLOW, GPTSwarm
extraction.key_results: DeepSeek-V3 backbone: AgentNet 92.86 MATH / 94.00 BBH / 30.00 API-Bank, best or second in every column; centralized MetaGPT reached only 64.00 BBH (DeepSeek-V3) and 53.00 (GPT-4o-mini). Several multi-agent baselines underperform single-agent prompting (MorphAgent 39.29 MATH vs Synapse 89.28 on DeepSeek-V3). Router ablation: 82.14% training / 86.00% test accuracy on BBH, above randomized routing variants. Removing the evolution phase drops MATH 85.00 to 77.86, API-Bank 32.00 to 23.00, BBH 86.00 to 76.00. Heterogeneity hurts at 3 agents (0.86 homogeneous vs 0.81 both-hetero) but helps at 5 agents (0.79 vs 0.85). Scaling from 3 agents/30 executors to 9 agents/40 executors gives only 80.38 to 81.18 training accuracy (diminishing returns).
extraction.limitations: Performance under heterogeneous agent capabilities, workflows, tools, and data remains an open question and may introduce coordination overhead; the router selects from a relatively small predefined candidate pool and its behaviour at hundreds or thousands of agents is unstudied; incentives for exploring agents beyond the predefined set are future work; no software-engineering benchmark is evaluated.

evidence_notes.finding: Router-driven dispatch to domain-expert agents beat both a single strong agent (95.00% vs 86.25% shallow foundations; 90.63% vs 87.50% pile design with Grok 3) and conventional fixed designer-checker multi-agent workflows by 10.0-43.75 points, while the fixed sequential multi-agent workflows actually underperformed the plain single agent, and the router configuration also had the lowest run-to-run variance.
evidence_notes.quote: Perfect scores (100.00%) consistently showed zero standard deviation, suggesting deterministic reasoning paths when models achieve complete problem understanding despite the probabilistic generation process.

extraction.framework: router-based multi-agent framework with dual-tier task classification and specialized domain-expert agents (Grok 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro backbones)
extraction.agent_count: 1 router plus specialized expert agents; the compared designer-checker workflows use 2 agents
extraction.benchmark: 27 foundation-design test cases across seven categories (shallow foundation and pile design), each executed in triple trials
extraction.baseline: single-agent processing with DeepSeek R1, ChatGPT 4 Turbo, Grok 3, and Gemini 2.5 Pro; conventional Agentic Workflow I and II (designer-checker)
extraction.key_results: Router workflow with Grok 3: 95.00% shallow foundation and 90.63% pile design, +8.75 and +3.13 points over standalone Grok 3 (86.25% / 87.50%) and 10.0-43.75 points over conventional workflows. With Gemini 2.5 Pro: 82.50% and 84.38%. Conventional Agentic Workflow I underperformed even single agents (38.75% shallow with Gemini 2.5 Pro; 51.56% pile). Router configuration achieved the lowest variance (SD 1.73% shallow, 3.25% pile) while weak configurations exceeded 8.0% SD. Perfect 100% performance on Pile Group analysis with both backbones vs 50.00-68.75% for conventional workflows.
extraction.limitations: Only 27 test cases across seven categories, giving limited statistical power (standard error roughly +/-4-6 points, so differences must exceed about 8-10 points to be reliable); results are presented as preliminary and needing validation on 100+ cases and independent replication; scope limited to shallow and pile foundations, excluding mat foundations, combined footings, and pile-raft systems; safety-critical use still requires continued human oversight.

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent teacher-student prompt-refinement system consistently outperformed single-LLM baselines (Mixtral-8x7B, Llama-2-7b, GPT-4o, Gemma-2-2b) on ROUGE and cosine similarity for software document summarization, and an adaptive stopping strategy cut training from 620 to 260 iterations with comparable quality, though the authors note multi-agent orchestration still adds computational overhead.
evidence_notes.quote: Despite the efficiency gains achieved by the dynamic iteration strategy, the orchestration of multiple LLM-based agents inevitably introduces computational overhead.

extraction.framework: Metagente, an LLM-based multi-agent system with a Teacher-Student prompt-optimization loop and dynamic stopping
extraction.agent_count: 4 LLM-based agents (including Summarizer Agent and Teacher Agent)
extraction.benchmark: GitHub README-to-About summarization and Google Play HTML app-description summarization datasets (D1, D2), scored with ROUGE-1/2/L and cosine similarity
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLMs Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, Llama-2-7b-hf, GPT-4o, and Gemma-2-2b-it; earlier GitSum (BART/T5)
extraction.key_results: Metagente consistently outperforms all single-agent baselines across ROUGE and cosine similarity on both datasets; Metagente ROUGE-L mostly ranges 0.3-1.0 on D1 while Mixtral and Llama-2-7b stay below 0.2, and Mixtral's ROUGE scores are mostly under 0.15 with high variance. The dynamic iteration strategy converged in 260 iterations versus 620 for the non-dynamic variant with comparable ROUGE and stronger cosine similarity, while reducing flow duration, step duration, and input/output token counts.
extraction.limitations: Evaluation limited to GitHub README and Google Play descriptions in English, so generalization to requirement specifications, technical reports, or bug reports is untested; ROUGE and cosine similarity may not capture semantic fidelity, factual consistency, or user-perceived usefulness; Google Play 'About' ground truth is marketing-oriented; possible overlap with LLM pre-training corpora could inflate results; Teacher-Student loop is sensitive to iteration thresholds and ROUGE cutoffs; single-agent baselines are sensitive to prompt and hyperparameter setup, affecting comparison fairness; multi-agent orchestration adds computational cost at scale.
